source.title: Evaluating Double Descent in Machine Learning: Insights from Tree-Based Models Applied to a Genomic Prediction Task

record.tranche_reason: The study tests double descent in tree-based models and argues that it appears under composite complexity scaling but resolves into separate U- and L-shaped patterns when complexity axes are varied independently.
record.gate_note: The study reports results from sweeps of learner capacity and ensemble size on genomic and synthetic data. Cited findings from other work and stated hyperparameter grids are not study results. Exact values visible only in the figures are not transcribed; figure rows use the authors' textual descriptions where available.
record.test_reason: It sweeps tree, random-forest and boosting capacity on genomic and synthetic data. Joint learner-capacity-then-ensemble scaling gives double descent (V4). Varying each axis alone gives U- or L-shaped curves, which bears on the axis-unfolding part of V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that double descent emerges only under composite scaling, not when either axis varies alone. They take this as support for Curth et al.'s unfolding hypothesis. They also say ensemble size acts as an implicit regulariser and that ensembles can overfit when learner capacity grows without variance control.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses test MSE and systematic complexity sweeps inspired by prior double-descent frameworks, but applies them to decision trees, random forests, and gradient boosting on genomic and synthetic data rather than testing the original deep-network settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed pattern depends on how complexity is scaled: composite capacity-then-ensemble sweeps show double descent, while isolated learner-capacity and ensemble-size sweeps show U- or L-shaped patterns.
record.problems: The study is restricted to tree-based classical learners and two datasets. It reports no uncertainty estimates. Some curve values and conditions are available only in figures or are not specified in the text; the interpolation threshold is marked in figures but its numerical location is not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separately stated numeric results were left out. Exact figure-only values were not extracted.

untested.parts: Only tree-based models. No kernels, linear models or other classes.
No single complexity measure predicting peak location.
Label noise and tuned regularization not varied. P_ens is called an implicit regulariser but is not tested as such.
No effective-parameter count is computed. The curve is not replotted against effective complexity.

missing.what: Tree/RF single-axis sweeps on synthetic data (MSE vs P_leaf at fixed P_ens; MSE vs P_ens at fixed P_leaf). The text only says these were replicated.
P_leaf sweeps at P_ens = 5, 10, 50 and boosting sweeps at P_ens > 1. These are run but have no reported values.

record.verdict_notes: Single-author preprint with one 70:30 split and a fixed seed. No uncertainty is reported, and only n=500 per dataset is used. The interpolation threshold is marked only in the figures. The design follows Curth et al. (a non-original source), so it is effectively a replication of the unfolding argument in a new biological setting.

versions.untested_parts: The study did not sweep training epochs or measure test error over training time.
Training sample size was not varied.

The study covers decision-tree-based and gradient-boosting models on one genomic task and one synthetic benchmark; it does not test all model classes or establish a general result beyond these settings.
No single measure of effective model complexity is proposed or tested as a predictor of peak location.
The study does not vary label noise or tune regularization to test whether peaks split or disappear.

The study argues that collapsing complexity axes can create an apparent double-descent curve, but does not measure an appropriate effective parameter count or show that the curve becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve when plotted against it.
